title: Which quintessential director is missing from this list?

commenti.body: [removed]

Off the jump you’ve missed Buster Keaton. I’d also put in James Cameron and Steven Spielberg if you’re going to understand perfect Hollywood blockbusters. Plus even Spielberg’s misses are a film school in themselves. 

I’d make sure to put in some trash as well. You can’t appreciate the good stuff if you don’t see the bad. I’d include Roger Corman and Paul W S Anderson. I’d also throw in John Waters, the king of trash. 

I’m sure there’s some obvious others to add but that’s what I’d start with.

Second the John waters add

Preston Sturges is one of the greatest writer directors ever with scripts like Sullivans travels and lady eve being considered some of the best films ever made.

Woody allen and Roman Polanski are controversial figures but their movies are some of the best you’ll find in the American new wave era (Chinatown and Annie Hall being two of the all time greats of that era)

Peter Bogdanovich is also someone that should be on the list, particularly for his 70s period where he made Targets, Last Picture show, What’s up doc, and Paper Moon. Fantastic film scholar and director of the period.

I would also add the two other silent clowns to the list: Harold Lloyd and Buster Keaton. Keaton is probably the more known and his films like Sherlock jr and the General are considered two of the best films ever. Lloyd is very much an underrated figure but his movies are still hilarious and his Everyman stories are still effective today in films like saftey last (which has one of the most iconic scenes of the silent era), the Freshman, Speedy and the kid brother.

Sergei Eisenstein pioneered montage. Totally terrible personal lives, but Roman Polanski and Woody Allen are important too I think. Nicolas Roeg. Steve McQueen. Peter Jackson. Danny Boyle. Peter Weir. Terry Gillam. Pasolini. Cronenberg. Haneke. Ang Lee. Jonze. Takashi Kitano. Wachowski sisters. Takashi Miike.   
Brian de Palma is important in New Hollywood. Animation: Ralph Bakshi, John Lasseter,   
Zemeckis for visual effects. Werner Herzog. Korean cinema: Park Chan Wook, Lee Chang Dong, Kim Ki-duk. Richard Linklater and Jarmusch for American independent cinema. Kubrick would also include Elia Kazan, David Lean, Max Ophuls as influences.

There are some glaring omissions though, some of which have been mentioned in previous comments:  Steven Spielberg, Robert Zemeckis, George Lucas, Brian DePalma, Oliver Stone, Jim Jarmusch, Ken Russell, David Cronenberg, Richard Donner, Ivan Reitman, Werner Herzog, Michael Cimino, John Houston, Roman Polanski, Woody Allen, Darren Aronofsky, just to name a few

Nuri Bilge Ceylan

One could definitely make a good argument about him being the greatest living director right now.

I think what Nuri Bilge Ceylan stated once is something that many films and most notably American films need to learn from, in relation to film conventions. American films always have to tie everything off in a nice bow, we can thank Spielberg for this. Not only this, they often involve "neatly packaged lessons", Nuri said "They want a life coach, I’m just trying to show life as I feel it.”

He understands the human condition, and that's why his films are infinitely interesting.

George Lucas does belong on any list of great directors.

Before adding anything, I'll instantly remove these directors from the list: Alfonso Cuaron, Bong Jong-ho, Jane Campion, Michael Bay, David Fincher, Christopher Nolan, Guillermo del Toro, Pedro Almodovar, Spike Lee, Edgar Wright.

There are lots that I would love to add, but it would be a crime if these names are missed: Luis Bunuel, Masaki Kobayashi, Werner Herzog, Mikhail Kalatozov, Jacques Tati, Hiroshi Teshigahara, Satoshi Kon.

Adrian Lyne. John Waters. They were both masters in their genres. Lyne was a genius at sex in film, sexual tension. His films are iconic. Watching his evolution is so rewarding. From Flashdance to Unfaithful. He gives everyone their voice. Fatal Attraction, 9 1/2 weeks. 

And John Waters is the king of camp. And filth. Every film he made is a gem and a dirty experience. You’ve got to watch each one!
Denis Villenueve?

You're gonna make some people angry if you include Godard but not Truffaut! Other than that, the directors I'd say you 100% need to add are:

- Sergueï Eisenstein, major figure of the Soviet cinema and its editing school.

- Robert Bresson, whose minimalist work is often cited as an inspiration by many filmmakers.

- Agnès Varda, probably the most famous female filmmaker and the "mother of the French New Wave".

- Warner Rainer Fassbinder, one of the most emblematic figures of the New German Cinema

- Ousmane Sembène, pioneer of African auteur cinema

- Luchino Visconti, major figure of Italian neorealism and director of some of the most remarkable historical dramas

- Steven Spielberg, whose work shaped the modern Hollywoodian blockbuster as we know it

- Luis Buñuel, the master of surrealism and sharp political satire


Otherwise, I'd suggest you consider Resnais, Wenders, Lubitsch, Murnau, Dreyer, Cronenberg, Mondo, Pasolini, Lean, Tarr, Ackerman, Mizoguchi, Keaton and Herzog in no particular order.

Some obvious names not names yet (at least at the moment i do this post):

Apart from that, it globally lacks international directors.

Only one Indian director seems not enough, for instance: your call on which one to add (Raj Kapoor, Guru Dutt, Bimal Roy, Adoor Gopalakrishnan...), even if it's not always easy because some only have done 2/3 great films only.

No African director either. I would at least put Youssef Chahine in there, considering his huge career. And at least one sub-saharian director (Cissé and/or Sembene would be the most obvious choices).

Latin America need also more names. At least Emilio Fernandez for the classical era, and Lucrecia Martel for contemporary era.

Documentary and experimental filmmakers are also missing, if I'm not mistaken. Even keeping it to the US, there are really big names: at least Frederick Wiseman for documentaries, and Maya Deren and Stan Brakhage for experimental.

And finally, in "genre cinema", I would add Seijun Suzuki or Shunya Itō for Japan, Mario Bava or Dario Argento for Italy, and Terence Fisher for UK (I see someone already named the HK big genre director).

Jacques Tati should be on there somewhere. It's hard to think of a funnier director, and Playtime is a work of mad genius.

Also William Friedkin is an important name in action/thriller/horror movies.

Also consider: Agnes Varda, Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Mira Nair, Ousmane Sembene, Seijun Suzuki, Tsui Hark, Zhang Yimou.

Is this list supposed to be aimed at a certain age group? Let's take De Sica for example. Shoeshine would be great for older kids, Bicycle Thieves for younger kids, Miracle in Milan for teens, and Umberto D for adults and those with dogs. You're missing Robert Bresson (he instructed his actors, usually not professionals, to not act; and his films are like moving mosaics; Carl Dreyer (like Ozu and Bresson, he's another director the writer of Taxi Driver considers sublime; he had an interesting approach to set design, where he kept removing pieces until only what he thought was essential remained) Mizoguchi, Kobayashi. Preston Sturges and Ernst Lubitsch are underrated and Hawks is overrated as far as comedy goes, imo. Jean Vigo had a short career, but Zero For Conduct is a pioneering coming of age film and L'atalante is possibly the most romantic movie ever made. Charles Laughton only got to direct the initially underrated film The Night of the Hunter. 

DW Griffith, according to Scorsese, developed the grammar of cinema. If I was to choose one film of his for young people to see, it would be True Heart Susie. Birth is great, but the dissonance from the greatness of the filmmaking and the ugly narrative sickened me. He made Intolerance to make up for it, but that's a little complex for an introduction. I loved Broken Blossoms, which was progressive for its day in portraying the love of a mixed race couple; the Orientalism and yellow face don't hold up, but considering a white actress won an Oscar for playing a Chinese man in the 80's (Mel Gibson didn't want to work with the real Chinese man who was going to play the part).

You should also have Truffaut (400 blows), Bunuel (The Forgotten Ones), Romero, Marcel Carne, Ken Russel (The Devils is like The Wicker Man, but leagues better and not for kids), Kieslowski (The Decalogue would make a stone cry), Hal Ashby (Harold and Maude), Nicholos Ray (Johnny Guitar), David Lean (Lawrence of Arabia), Sidney Lumet (Network), Robert Altman (Secret Honor is my favorite, although he has about five much more acclaimed movies), Visconti (Rocco and His Brothers), Lynch (The Straight Story), Jacques Becker (Le Trou), Murnau (Sunrise), Kore eda (Shoplifters has nudity), Yuasa (he may be the next Miyazaki - The Night is Short Walk on Girl), Clouzot (The Wages of Fear).

Yes that’s correct.. what was I thinking!

Hiroshi Shimizu: Primarily a silent filmmaker, he was a close friend of Ozu and one of the biggest names in Japanese cinema throughout the 30s. Not the most accessible library, but he shot on location a lot and I would say he captures that older culture of Japan better than either Ozu or Kurosawa.

Michael Curtiz: Primarily known for Casablanca, but his filmography is extremely diverse and full of a lot of studio-era gems that show off the beautiful sets and performances of the Golden Age in Hollywood.

Satoshi Kon: Considered by many to be the greatest storyteller of the anime medium. He died tragically young, but in his life put out four feature length films that are *all* heralded as the best of their class, with two being obvious inspirations for some of today's biggest directors (those being Perfect Blue and Paprika). Personally, I think he's one of the best directors to ever live.

George A. Romero: One of the most influential directors of all time. He invented an entirely new genre of horror with his zombie, a cross between the classical undead and vampires. He established it in Night, perfected it with Dawn and then pushed the envelope as far as it could go with Day. If you're only going to have one voice for horror (you have Carpenter already, at least), it's him.

Jim Jarmusch: In terms of contemporary American directors, I believe he stands in the same tier as Scorsese and Lynch. His style is undeniable and his films range from iconic to intensely quiet and personal. He takes on the "loser" archetype a lot, but really anything works when he's at the helm. For perspective, his first work is Permanent Vacation, in which he already completely mastered his vision for storytelling and the kinds of narratives he wanted to weave.

Jean Cocteau: In my opinion, the greatest director to come from France. One of the best artists of the 20th century. Cocteau was, and still is even by today's standards, a revolutionary in his combination of film, poetry and the arts within his works. The Orphic Trilogy (Blood of a Poet, Orpheus and Testament of Orpheus) make for the greatest trio of movies ever and when I promise you there's no one else like him, believe me that it's true.

Roger Corman: You can't tell the story of independent cinema, or even just modern cinema, without Corman, who funded/produced over 200 movies and directed another 50. He kickstarted the careers of Jack Nicholson, Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola and Peter Bogdanovich. The French New Wave class of creators all held him in the highest possible regard and he directly inspired the American New Wave movement in the late 60s. Cassavetes may have singlehandedly invented what we generally see as "indie" nowadays, but Corman is the one who gave young directors free reign on limited budget to make whatever they wanted.
